business_summary: Microsoft sells software, cloud computing and devices to businesses, governments and consumers, mostly as multi-year subscriptions and metered cloud usage. In fiscal 2026 (year ended 2026-06-30) it reported revenue of $331.839B (+17.8% YoY) across three reported segments: Productivity & Business Processes $139.996B (Microsoft 365, Teams, LinkedIn, Dynamics), Intelligent Cloud $137.791B (Azure, server products, GitHub), and More Personal Computing $54.052B (Windows, Xbox, Surface, search advertising). Microsoft Cloud revenue passed $214B (+27%) and Azure passed $100B for the first time (+41% for the year, +43% in Q4). Commercial remaining performance obligation - contracted revenue not yet recognised - was $684B at 2026-06-30 versus $375B a year earlier. Microsoft 365 Copilot passed 30 million paid seats. Effective FY2027 Microsoft reports in two segments, 'Agents and Infra' (FY2026 restated revenue $268.1B, operating income $136.4B) and 'Devices and Consumer' ($63.7B / $18.9B). The business should still be winning in 5-10 years because enterprises run their core operations, identity and data on Microsoft software, switching costs are very high, and Microsoft owns both the distribution and a large share of the AI compute build-out. The central open question is no longer growth - it is whether the enormous capital now being sunk into AI infrastructure ($115.948B of property-and-equipment additions in FY2026 alone) earns an adequate return.

moat.type: High switching costs (Microsoft 365, Windows, Entra ID, Dynamics), network effects (Teams, LinkedIn, GitHub), scale economies in cloud infrastructure, and unmatched enterprise distribution now being used to push AI/Copilot into an installed base it already owns

quality.gross_margin: 67.9% FY2026 (gross profit $225.465B / revenue $331.839B), down from 68.8% in FY2025 - cloud/AI infrastructure is diluting mix
quality.roic: ~26% FY2026 computed (NOPAT $125.1B = operating income $155.237B x (1 - 19.4% effective tax rate); invested capital $472.4B = equity $442.387B + debt $40.294B + finance leases $66.594B - cash & short-term investments $76.843B). Down from ~31% on the same end-of-period basis in FY2025 as capital intensity rises.
quality.net_debt_to_ebitda: ~0.15x including finance leases (net debt $30.0B = $40.294B debt + $66.594B finance leases - $76.843B cash & ST investments; EBITDA ~$199.6B = operating income $155.237B + depreciation $34.3B + intangible amortization $4.7B + finance-lease ROU amortization $5.403B). Excluding finance leases Microsoft is in a $36.5B net cash position.
quality.fcf_positive: yes, but shrinking: FY2026 FCF $66.987B (operating cash flow $182.935B - capex $115.948B) versus $71.611B in FY2025. Net income rose 31% while free cash flow fell 6%.

valuation.method: Blend of two methods, averaged by code/valuation.py. (1) P/E on FY2026 non-GAAP diluted EPS of $17.28 at 24x / 28x / 32x -> $414.72 / $483.84 / $552.96. Non-GAAP EPS is used instead of GAAP $17.95 because GAAP includes a $4.963B net gain from OpenAI investments. 28x is the centre because Microsoft is a ~18%-growth, 47%-operating-margin, net-cash compounder, but capital intensity is rising fast. (2) FCF yield on FY2026 FCF per share of $8.99 ($66.987B / 7,453M diluted shares) at 3.5% / 3.0% / 2.5% -> $256.86 / $299.67 / $359.60. The two methods disagree sharply and that disagreement is the thesis: earnings look excellent while free cash flow is being consumed by an unproven AI capex cycle. We keep both, which gives a deliberately wide and humble band. Sensitivity: P/E-only would give $415 / $484 / $553; at $493.13 even that leaves no margin of safety.

bull_case: Growth reaccelerated, not decelerated: FY2026 revenue +17.8% to $331.839B, operating income +21% to $155.237B, with quarterly revenue growth of +18.4% / +16.7% / +18.3% / +18.4% through the year - unusual for a company this size.
Azure passed $100B of annual revenue and still grew 41% for FY2026 (+43% in Q4), and Microsoft Cloud passed $214B (+27%).

Demand is contracted, not hoped for: commercial remaining performance obligation reached $684B at 2026-06-30 versus $375B a year earlier, and management guides FY27 Q1 revenue of $89.85-$90.95B (~+16% versus FY26 Q1's $77.673B).
AI is monetising through the existing installed base: Microsoft 365 Copilot passed 30 million paid seats and the AI business passed a $37B annual run rate (+123% YoY) as of Q3 FY2026.
Still exceptional economics: 67.9% gross margin, 46.8% operating margin, ~26% ROIC, and a net-cash balance sheet excluding finance leases; $26.4B of dividends and $22.3B of buybacks paid in FY2026.

Wide, durable moat: enterprises are locked into Microsoft 365, Windows, Entra ID and Dynamics with very high switching costs, and Microsoft controls the distribution channel through which AI reaches those customers.
risks: Valuation: at $493.13 the stock sits ~26% ABOVE our base fair value of $391.75 and above the high end of the band ($456.28). There is no margin of safety; this is a watch-and-wait name, not a buy at this price.

The capex cycle is the dominant risk. Property-and-equipment additions went $44.477B (FY2024) -> $64.551B (FY2025) -> $115.948B (FY2026), and FY27 Q1 alone is guided to 'over $50 billion'. Free cash flow already fell from $71.611B to $66.987B while net income rose 31%. The CFO has guided only to Microsoft remaining free-cash-flow POSITIVE in FY2027, which implies FCF could be very small.

Depreciation is a delayed bill. Depreciation rose from $22.0B (FY2025) to $34.3B (FY2026) and will keep climbing; if AI revenue does not scale to match, reported earnings - not just cash flow - get hit in FY2028-FY2029. Management has also changed asset useful lives, which flatters near-term earnings and deserves scrutiny.

Capital intensity is eroding returns: ROIC fell from ~31% to ~26% and gross margin from 68.8% to 67.9% in one year. Microsoft is becoming a more capital-hungry, lower-return business than the software company it was.
Off-balance-sheet-style leverage is growing: finance lease liabilities rose from $27.145B (FY2024) to $46.172B (FY2025) to $66.594B (FY2026). Headline 'net cash' understates the real commitments.

GAAP earnings quality is noisier: FY2026 GAAP net income of $133.749B includes a $4.963B net gain from OpenAI investments and a $3.2B gain on the Anthropic investment in Q4. Mark-to-market investment swings now move reported EPS materially in both directions.
More Personal Computing is shrinking (-4% in Q4 FY2026, $54.052B for the year), so essentially all growth depends on cloud and AI.

Concentration, regulation and competition: an AI demand air-pocket, antitrust scrutiny of cloud bundling and the OpenAI relationship, or aggressive pricing from AWS/Google Cloud would all hit the growth engine at once.
The FY2027 segment reorganisation into two segments reduces reporting granularity, making it harder to track the health of individual businesses over time.
what_would_break_thesis: Azure (or the successor 'Agents and Infra' segment) revenue growth falls below 15% year-over-year for two consecutive quarters.
Free cash flow turns negative for a full fiscal year, or falls below $40B in a fiscal year, without a clearly communicated and credible capex-normalisation plan.
Total revenue declines year-over-year for two consecutive quarters.
Company-wide gross margin falls below 60% for two consecutive quarters.
Operating margin falls below 35% for two consecutive quarters (evidence that AI depreciation is overwhelming the P&L).
Net-debt-to-EBITDA, including finance lease liabilities, rises above 1.5x.
ROIC (computed the same way as in this thesis) falls below 15% for two consecutive fiscal years.
A large asset impairment or write-down of AI/data-centre assets, or a change in asset useful lives that is used to mask deteriorating economics.
A serious accounting restatement, auditor change under dispute, or material governance red-flag event.
catalysts: FY2027 Q1 earnings expected late October 2026: the first read on whether 'over $50B' of quarterly capex is being matched by Azure and Copilot revenue, and the first report under the new two-segment structure.
Evidence of capex normalisation or an explicit return-on-AI-investment disclosure, which would let the FCF-yield method converge upward toward the P/E method.
Continued conversion of the $684B remaining performance obligation into recognised revenue at high margin.

A price pullback toward the $392 base or the $336 low end of the fair-value band, which would open a real margin of safety; a drawdown driven by AI-capex fear rather than by a break in the operating business would be the opportunity we are waiting for.
